chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
title: The Bebop versus Dixieland split and the role of disc jockeys and the press
summary: He thinks the split between Moldy Figs and Bebop came from disc jockeys and the press, not musicians, who are all friends.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: But you know, what happened, what seemed to have happened in the mid-Forties, when Bop came on the scene, and I don't know for what reason this happened, and it will be interesting knowing what you felt about it... When the split developed, or the seeming split, where everything was either something like Dixieland or Moldy Fig, or Bebop or Modern, you know, whatever, and people started putting one thing down...
Yeah. Yes, they did.
Did that come from the musicians? Or was it economic things? Or was it something that...

I really don't know. I guess it came from both. And a lot came from when we had record players, the disk jockeys. Some disk jockeys wouldn't play nothin' but that. They refused to play anything but that. I don't want to name names, but you know...
Dickenson - 153
Right.

So it prejudices people against other types of music. I don't know what's wrong with disk jockeys. They keep playing the same thing over and over and over. Every day you hear the same... Instead of changing it, putting different types of music on and different things on. No, they keep playing the same thing, you'd hear the same thing every day, in and out.
It's because they want to make hits, and so they saturate...

Yes. But I mean, they should give the people a chance to hear something else sometimes. I don't care -- whatever type of music it is. They should change it around a little bit, give everybody a chance to hear it. They knock(?) people from listening to their channels, because a lot of people get mad at them because they get themselves stuck in one rut. And there must be somebody hiring... It don't have to be the disk jockey that does it. It's the people that tells them what to play.
Yes, that's the thing

And I don't think that should be. I think the disk jockey should have the choice of playing, instead of somebody saying, 'You've got to play this.' That's wrong. Because that shows that there's a payoff somewhere,
Dickenson - 154
and that's not...
Well, it isn't...
There's some word I want to use.
Well, it's not right. It's not kosher, that's right. So you feel that that had something to do with those days, too.
I think it did. Quite a bit. I certainly do.
Then you would also read a lot of things in the magazines...
Yes. The magazines did it, too, just the same as the disk jockeys.
So you don't really feel that it was the musicians who started splitting into camps.
No, I never did. No. All musicians are friends.
[END OF TAPE 5, SIDE A]
Yeah, it's always seemed that way to me.

You would see things... I look at old issues of Downbeat, and you see things like some bandleader saying, 'Bebop is hurting the business because they're playing music that people can't understand, and it turns them away from
Dickenson - 155
Jazz and so on."

Yeah. Or "Jazz is too square." It's really the press that never got it. And they're the ones that did it. The people as a whole didn't, and neither did the musicians. But some guys that wanted to capitalize on something, you know...
